name: Sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
aliases: aneurysm of the sinus of Valsalva

reference.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease / ESC guidelines on aortic disease
clinicalPearls: An abnormal dilatation of one of the aortic sinuses, most often the right coronary sinus, arising from congenital weakness of the aortic wall at the sinus or from acquired causes
Unruptured aneurysms are frequently asymptomatic and found incidentally, though a large one may compress adjacent structures or distort the aortic valve
Rupture is the feared complication and usually drains into a low-pressure right-sided chamber, most commonly the right ventricle or right atrium, creating a left-to-right shunt
Acute rupture can present with sudden chest pain, breathlessness, and a continuous murmur, and may precipitate heart failure
A continuous murmur from a ruptured aneurysm can be mistaken for a patent ductus arteriosus or a coronary arteriovenous fistula
It is associated with connective tissue disorders, bicuspid aortic valve, and ventricular septal defect, and may follow infective endocarditis or trauma
Echocardiography, particularly transoesophageal, together with CT or MRI and cardiac catheterisation define the anatomy and any shunt
Symptomatic, ruptured, or enlarging aneurysms are treated by surgical or, in selected cases, transcatheter repair
reference.pathophysiology: A sinus of Valsalva aneurysm results from a deficiency in the elastic and muscular tissue where the aortic media meets the annulus fibrosus, allowing the affected aortic sinus to bulge. The weakness may be congenital or acquired through infection such as endocarditis, connective tissue disease, atherosclerosis, or trauma. Over time the thin-walled aneurysm enlarges under aortic pressure and may compress neighbouring structures or interfere with the aortic valve and coronary ostia. If the wall gives way, blood jets from the high-pressure aorta into an adjacent lower-pressure chamber, most often on the right side of the heart, establishing a left-to-right shunt with volume overload and, if large, acute heart failure.
additionalDifferentials: Ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation
Ruptured aortic dissection into a cardiac chamber
Aortic root aneurysm from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography with Doppler to define the aneurysm and detect a shunt
CT or MRI angiography of the aortic root to delineate anatomy and relationships
Cardiac catheterisation to quantify shunt and assess coronary anatomy before intervention
ECG and chest radiograph as initial assessment for chamber enlargement or pulmonary plethora
Evaluation for associated lesions such as bicuspid valve, ventricular septal defect, and connective tissue disease
Blood cultures where infective endocarditis is suspected as a cause
redFlags: Acute rupture with chest pain, breathlessness, and a new continuous murmur
Rapid onset of heart failure from a large left-to-right shunt
Compression of coronary ostia causing ischaemia
Conduction disturbance from an aneurysm involving the interventricular septum
reference.prognosis: Unruptured aneurysms may remain stable for years, but rupture carries significant risk and, if untreated, can lead to progressive heart failure; surgical or transcatheter repair generally has good outcomes when performed promptly.
pitfalls: Attributing a continuous murmur to a patent ductus arteriosus rather than a ruptured aneurysm
Missing an incidental unruptured aneurysm that warrants surveillance
Overlooking associated lesions such as ventricular septal defect or bicuspid aortic valve
Delaying repair once rupture or significant enlargement is evident
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases
management: Surgical repair with patch closure of the defect and aortic root repair, adding aortic valve repair or replacement where needed, is the definitive treatment for ruptured or symptomatic aneurysms
Transcatheter device closure as an alternative for selected ruptured aneurysms with suitable anatomy
Stabilisation of acute rupture with diuretics and afterload reduction for heart failure while expediting repair
Prompt treatment of infective endocarditis where implicated, with attention to endocarditis prevention
Surveillance of unruptured aneurysms with serial echocardiography and cross-sectional imaging for enlargement or valve or coronary compromise
Evaluation and management of associated lesions such as bicuspid aortic valve, ventricular septal defect and connective tissue disease
Coordinated cardiology and cardiac surgery input
